body:
Epic and temple-based theatre

Southern India has several theatrical traditions in which music, dance, elaborate costumes, religious narratives and dramatic acting are closely integrated. Many developed around temples and regional religious institutions.

These forms illustrate how Sanskrit literary traditions and regional cultural practices can combine. For example, the temple theatre of Kerala has long drawn material from Sanskrit epics while developing distinctive regional performance traditions.

Kutiyattam: the living Sanskrit theatre tradition

Kutiyattam, also written as Koodiyattam, is a traditional Sanskrit theatre form of Kerala. It preserves an important living connection with India's classical dramatic heritage.

Its traditional performances take place in temple theatres known as Koothambalams. Sanskrit dramatic texts, expressive acting, music and elaborate presentation are central features.

Kutiyattam has traditionally been associated with Chakyar performers, Nangiar women performers and Nambiar musicians. The Mizhavu, a large percussion instrument, is especially associated with this tradition.

Chakyar Koothu is a related Kerala tradition in which a solo performer narrates and interprets stories, often including humour and social commentary. It should not be treated as identical to Kutiyattam, which is a broader dramatic performance tradition involving multiple characters.

Kutiyattam was proclaimed a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2001 and was incorporated into the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

Other major southern theatrical forms

FormRegionPrincipal feature
YakshaganaKarnatakaEpic-based dance-drama
TherukoothuTamil NaduStreet theatre and Mahabharata narratives
Bhagavata MelaTamil NaduDevotional dance-drama
KrishnattamKeralaEpisodes from Krishna's life
MudiyettuKeralaCommunity ritual theatre

Yakshagana

Yakshagana is particularly associated with coastal Karnataka. It combines singing, music, dance and dramatic dialogue with distinctive costumes and headgear.

Its stories commonly draw upon the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas. The Bhagavata, or principal singer-narrator, helps carry the narrative forward.

Yakshagana also influenced the costumes and stories of Karnataka's traditional string puppetry. Nevertheless, Yakshagana performed by human actors and Yakshagana-based puppet theatre are distinct forms of performance.

Therukoothu and Bhagavata Mela

The term Therukoothu broadly means street theatre. It is particularly associated with Tamil Nadu and village festival performances. Episodes concerning Draupadi and the Mahabharata occupy an important place in its repertoire.

Bhagavata Mela is a devotional dance-drama tradition associated especially with Melattur in Tamil Nadu. Performances commonly include Vaishnava narratives, particularly the story of Prahlada and Narasimha.

Krishnattam and Mudiyettu

Krishnattam developed in Kerala under the patronage of Manaveda, the Zamorin of Calicut, in the 17th century. It presents Krishna's life through a cycle of 8 plays and has a particularly important association with Guruvayur.

Mudiyettu is a ritual theatrical tradition of Kerala depicting the conflict between the goddess Kali and the demon Darika. It is performed in connection with religious observances and involves participation by the local community.

Important UNESCO inscriptions connected with theatre

UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity recognises living cultural practices, knowledge and expressions transmitted by communities. It is distinct from the World Heritage List, which recognises cultural and natural properties.

Important Indian theatrical and ritual performance traditions on the Representative List include:

  • Kutiyattam, Sanskrit theatre: Kerala; inscribed in 2008.
  • Ramlila, the traditional performance of the Ramayana: principally northern India; inscribed in 2008, following its earlier proclamation in 2005.
  • Ramman: Religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal Himalayas, Uttarakhand; inscribed in 2009.
  • Mudiyettu: Ritual theatre and dance drama of Kerala; inscribed in 2010.

Ramman and Ramlila

Ramman is a religious and theatrical festival associated with the villages of Saloor-Dungra in Uttarakhand. It includes masked performances, music and local ritual observances associated with the village deity.

Ramlila is the dramatic presentation of Rama's story and has a much wider geographical distribution. Despite the similarity of their names, Ramman and Ramlila are separate UNESCO-listed cultural expressions.

Prelims focus

  • Kutiyattam: Kerala, Sanskrit theatre, Koothambalam and Mizhavu.
  • Yakshagana: Karnataka; Therukoothu: Tamil Nadu.
  • Bhagavata Mela: Melattur, Tamil Nadu.
  • Krishnattam: Kerala and a cycle of 8 plays.
  • Ramman: Uttarakhand, inscribed in 2009; Mudiyettu: Kerala, inscribed in 2010.
  • Trap: UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage inscriptions are not World Heritage Site designations.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, 2020–21 edition, The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 122–123; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, p. 113; CCRT, Traditional Theatre Forms of India, Cultural Package 17; Employment News, Different Forms of Traditional Theatre, 25–31 March 2023; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, individual entries for Kutiyattam, Ramlila, Ramman and Mudiyettu; inscription records consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Southern Indian Theatre and UNESCO-Recognised Traditions

body:
Bhavai: Gujarat's traditional folk theatre

Bhavai is a traditional Gujarati theatrical form that combines acting, songs, music, humour, satire and devotional elements. It developed as a popular means of entertainment and communication among rural and urban communities in Gujarat.

Bhavai has strong historical associations with northern Gujarat, Saurashtra and Kutch. Travelling performers helped spread its stories and social messages across different regions.

Asaita Thakar and the performing community

The origin of Bhavai is traditionally attributed to Asaita Thakar, also written as Asait Thakar, a poet and performer associated with Unjha in northern Gujarat during the 14th century.

The traditions surrounding his life contain legendary accounts, so their details should not all be treated as independently established historical events. His association with the development of Bhavai, however, occupies a central place in Gujarati cultural tradition.

The traditional performing community is known as the Targala or Bhavaiya community. These performers preserved dramatic stories, songs and other knowledge through family and community transmission.

Vesha and the structure of Bhavai

An individual dramatic episode or sketch in Bhavai is called a Vesha. A performance may include several veshas, each presenting particular characters and situations.

Themes may be religious, historical, humorous or social. Recognisable character types allow Bhavai to expose dishonesty, greed, hypocrisy, discrimination and other social problems.

Traditional veshas include Kajoda and Jhanda Jhulan. Kajoda, for example, uses humour and social situations to draw attention to problems associated with unequal or unsuitable marriage.

Ranglo is a comic figure associated with Bhavai. Ranglo and Rangli have also become familiar characters in later popular and educational presentations.

Performance setting and musical identity

Bhavai was traditionally performed in open spaces such as village squares and temple courtyards, often during the evening or night. A permanent theatre building and elaborate stage scenery were not essential.

Performances commonly begin with devotional elements associated with the Mother Goddess. The Bhungal, a long wind instrument, is particularly characteristic of Bhavai. Other musical instruments may include tabla, cymbals and various string and percussion instruments.

Social significance

Bhavai combines entertainment with criticism of society. Through recognisable local characters and accessible language, it communicates social messages to audiences without depending on formal education or literacy.

The same tradition can be adapted to communicate contemporary concerns, such as girls' education, social equality and public awareness. Its devotional origins therefore do not restrict all its subject matter to religious stories.

Bhavai theatre and Bhavai dance

Gujarati Bhavai is principally a folk theatre tradition. Rajasthan also has a performance tradition called Bhavai, commonly identified with dancers balancing pots. The identical name should not lead to confusion between the two regional forms.

The emergence of the modern Gujarati stage

During the 19th century, Gujarati theatre developed alongside the growth of professional stage companies in Bombay and Gujarat. This development introduced new dramatic scripts, commercial theatre performances and more elaborate stage arrangements.

Early Parsi theatre companies in Bombay used Gujarati among their performance languages. Professional Gujarati theatre subsequently developed its own companies, playwrights, actors and directors.

  • Ranchhodbhai Udayram Dave: An important pioneer of modern Gujarati drama and its literary development.
  • Morbi Arya Subodh Natak Mandali: Founded around 1878 by Waghji Asharam with the participation of his brother Moolji Asharam.
  • Deshi Natak Samaj: Founded by Dahyabhai Dholshaji Jhaveri in Ahmedabad in 1889.
  • Chandravadan Mehta: A playwright, actor and director who made important contributions to the development of modern and amateur Gujarati theatre.

Important personalities of Gujarati theatre

PersonalityPrincipal association
Jaishankar BhojakKnown as Jaishankar Sundari; celebrated actor
Amrut NayakActor and director, including work in Urdu theatre
Bapulal NayakActor and theatre director
Chandravadan MehtaPlaywriting and amateur theatre
Jashwant ThakerTheatre direction and Gujarati stage
Dina PathakActing and Gujarati theatre
Pravin JoshiModern Gujarati theatre direction
Upendra TrivediGujarati stage and cinema

Jaishankar Bhojak became popularly known as Sundari after his successful portrayal of the heroine in the play Saubhagya Sundari. This is an important example of the historical practice of male actors performing female roles on the professional stage.

The growth of modern Gujarati theatre did not eliminate Bhavai. Elements of folk humour, music, satire and regional storytelling continued to influence modern dramatic expression.

Prelims focus

  • Asaita Thakar: traditional founder of Bhavai, associated with Unjha.
  • Targala or Bhavaiya: traditional Bhavai performing community.
  • Vesha: an individual dramatic episode in Bhavai.
  • Bhungal: characteristic wind instrument of Bhavai.
  • Jaishankar Bhojak is popularly known as Jaishankar Sundari.
  • Trap: Gujarati Bhavai theatre and Rajasthani Bhavai pot-balancing dance are distinct traditions.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Standard 10 Social Science, English edition, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, pp. 14–15; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, p. 113; Indian Folklife, Vol. 2, Issue 1, July 2002, article on Bhavai; D. G. Vyas, Gujarati Drama, in Indian Drama, Publications Division, 1956, pp. 52–60; online copies consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Bhavai and the Development of Gujarati Theatre

body:
The emergence of modern theatre

During British rule, Indian theatre underwent important changes due to the growth of cities, printing, modern education, commercial entertainment and exposure to European dramatic traditions.

The establishment of professional theatre companies encouraged regular ticketed performances before urban audiences. Playwrights increasingly used written scripts to address historical subjects, social reform, colonial exploitation and contemporary political developments.

The proscenium stage

A proscenium theatre has a defined stage opening separating the main performance area from the audience. Curtains, scenery and lighting may be used to represent different settings.

This type of stage became influential in colonial urban theatre. It contrasts with several traditional folk theatre arrangements in which performers act in an open space surrounded wholly or partly by the audience.

Parsi theatre

Parsi theatre developed in 19th-century Bombay and became an important commercial theatrical tradition. Its professional companies travelled widely and helped spread modern stage entertainment across different parts of India.

Although its early development was closely associated with the Parsi community, its performers, playwrights and audiences eventually represented a much wider social and linguistic background.

Parsi theatre combined Indian stories and musical traditions with Western-influenced stage arrangements. Gujarati, Urdu and Hindustani were important performance languages. Songs, romance, mythology, historical stories, dramatic dialogue and elaborate scenery became characteristic features.

The playwright Agha Hashr Kashmiri made significant contributions to Urdu commercial theatre. The conventions of Parsi theatre also influenced early Indian cinema, particularly its combination of dramatic storytelling, music and popular entertainment.

Theatre as a medium of social reform and political resistance

Modern drama was not limited to entertainment. Playwrights used theatrical stories to expose social injustice and the effects of colonial rule.

Nil Darpan

Nil Darpan, written by Dinabandhu Mitra and published in 1860, is a Bengali play that depicts the exploitation of indigo cultivators by European indigo planters.

It is associated with the social conditions that produced the Indigo Revolt of 1859–1860. The play helped bring the sufferings of cultivators to a wider audience.

Dramatic Performances Act, 1876

The colonial government enacted the Dramatic Performances Act in 1876 to control certain theatrical performances. It empowered colonial authorities to prohibit performances considered objectionable under the provisions of the law, including those regarded as encouraging disaffection against the government.

The Act illustrates how theatre had become an influential means of political and public communication during colonial rule.

Indian People's Theatre Association

The Indian People's Theatre Association, commonly known as IPTA, was established in 1943. It developed as a cultural movement that employed theatre, music and other performing arts to address the concerns of ordinary people.

Its productions presented themes such as poverty, exploitation, famine, social inequality and the struggle for freedom.

Nabanna, written by Bijon Bhattacharya and staged in 1944, is an important example of this tradition. The Bengali play depicts suffering associated with the Bengal famine of 1943.

Important modern Indian playwrights

PlaywrightAssociated worksPrincipal language
Bharatendu HarishchandraAndher NagariHindi
Rabindranath TagoreDak Ghar, RaktakarabiBengali
Mohan RakeshAshadh Ka Ek Din, Adhe AdhureHindi
Dharamvir BharatiAndha YugHindi
Vijay TendulkarGhashiram Kotwal, Shantata! Court Chalu AaheMarathi
Girish KarnadTughlaq, Hayavadana, YayatiKannada
Badal SircarEvam Indrajit, Baki ItihasBengali
Habib TanvirAgra Bazaar, Charandas ChorHindustani and regional languages

Modern playwrights often combined new dramatic approaches with older Indian stories. Girish Karnad adapted historical and mythological material, while Dharamvir Bharati's Andha Yug uses the aftermath of the Mahabharata war to explore the consequences of destruction.

Mohan Rakesh's Ashadh Ka Ek Din presents an imagined dramatic account connected with Kalidasa's life. It is a modern Hindi play about a classical literary figure, rather than a Sanskrit drama written by Kalidasa.

Third Theatre and Naya Theatre

Badal Sircar is associated with Third Theatre, an approach that sought direct communication with audiences through relatively simple and flexible performance arrangements outside the conventional commercial stage.

Habib Tanvir founded Naya Theatre and became known for integrating folk performers and regional cultural traditions, particularly those of Chhattisgarh, into modern drama.

Institutions supporting theatre

InstitutionEstablishmentPrincipal function
Sangeet Natak Akademi1953Promotion and preservation of music, dance and drama
National School of Drama1959Professional theatre education and training

The National School of Drama was established under the Sangeet Natak Akademi and became an autonomous institution in 1975. It is located in New Delhi. Ebrahim Alkazi was an influential theatre director and served as director of the institution from 1962 to 1977.

Prelims focus

  • Parsi theatre developed in 19th-century Bombay.
  • Dinabandhu Mitra: Nil Darpan, published in 1860.
  • Dramatic Performances Act: 1876.
  • IPTA: established in 1943; Nabanna: Bijon Bhattacharya, staged in 1944.
  • Badal Sircar: Third Theatre; Habib Tanvir: Naya Theatre.
  • Trap: The National School of Drama was established in 1959 and became autonomous in 1975.

[References: CBSE, Knowledge Traditions and Practices of India, Class 11, Module 10, modern Indian theatre section; Kathryn Hansen, Languages on Stage: Linguistic Pluralism and Community Formation in the Nineteenth-Century Parsi Theatre, Modern Asian Studies; INFLIBNET, Comparative Indian Drama, colonial theatre sections; National School of Drama, institutional history and former directors; Sangeet Natak Akademi, institutional history; Oxford University Press, Three Modern Indian Plays; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
